core.text: When you speak to someone by name or title, that word goes into **the vocative (the calling form)**, *cāsus vocātīvus*: *Salvē, domine!* = Hello, master! *Tacē, Mēde!* Nearly always it looks exactly like the nominative (the plain naming form) — *Iūlia!*, *puerī!* — so there is one thing to learn: nouns in -us change to -e, and names in -ius (and *meus*) to -ī: *Mārce!*, *Iūlī!*, *mī fīlī!*
English marks the person addressed only with commas and the voice: *Bill, the cup is on the table.* Latin gives the name its own ending, which is why *Mārce* looks wrong at first.
Vocative = nominative, except 2nd-declension -us → -e (*serve*, *Dāve*) and -ius → -ī (*Iūlī*, *fīlī*). The plural is never different (*servī!*).

invented.la: Salvē, Iūlī! Ubi est fīlius tuus?
invented.en: Hello, Julius! Where is your son?

invented.la: Ō mī fīlī, venī ad mē!
invented.en: O my son, come to me!

core.text: *Mārcus venit* — Marcus is the subject, coming. *Mārce, venī!* — Marcus is being spoken to and told to come. A name in -e beside a command or a greeting is not a misspelling but the vocative; the subject of the command is 'you'.

more.text: From the learner's notes: direct address is calling out a name to get someone's attention, and it can sit inside a statement, a question or a command. The vocative is left out of most declension charts because it copies the nominative; only the two exceptions need remembering — -us → -e (*Marcus* → *Marce!*), and -ius or *meus* → -ī (*Iūlius* → *Iūlī!*, *meus* → *mī*).

Ørberg cap. IV: *Dāve!* vocātīvus -e. The vocative often comes second in its sentence, tucked after the first word (*Quid est, domine?*), and can follow *ō* (*Ō Iūlia, mea parva fīlia!*). Adjectives agreeing with it take -e too: *puer improbe!* *Mī* is the vocative of *meus*, but feminine *mea* does not change (*mea Lydia*). *Deus* keeps *deus* as its vocative. A&G §340.
